pg007_n0006: This textbook, Mathematics for Secondary Schools Form two, is written specifically for Form Two students in the United Republic of Tanzania.
pg007_n0007: The book is prepared in accordance with the 2023 Mathematics Syllabus for Ordinary Secondary Education, Form I–IV, issued by the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology.
pg007_n0008: It is a revised edition of Basic Mathematics for Secondary Schools Student’s Book Form Two that was published in 2021 in accordance with the 2005 syllabus issued by the then, Ministry of Education and Vocational Training (MoEVT).
pg007_n0010: The textbook consists of eight chapters, namely: Rates and variations, Congruence, Similarity, Algebra, Exponents and radicals, Logarithms, Sets, and Trigonometry.
pg007_n0011: In addition to the contents, each chapter contains activities, illustrations, projects, and exercises.
pg007_n0012: You are encouraged to do all the activities, and questions in the exercises.
pg007_n0013: This will enhance your understanding and development of the intended competencies for this level.

pg008_n0012: Understanding rates and variations is essential for grasping how quantities change in relation to each other.
pg008_n0013: Some variables are interdependent, meaning a change in one affects the others.
pg008_n0014: Many real-life situations involve such relationships.
pg008_n0015: In this chapter, you will describe the concepts of rates and variations, explain the types of variations, and solve problems on rates and variations.
pg008_n0016: The competencies developed will enable you to solve real-life challenges such as finding shopping deals, assessing fuel efficiency, or predicting data trends in fields like economics, science, engineering, and many other applications.

pg012_n0037: Variation is a relationship where a change in one quantity leads to a proportional change in the other.
pg012_n0038: It allows for the exploration of connections between two or more quantities.
pg012_n0039: The four basic types of variations are direct, inverse, joint, and combined.
pg013_n0005: Direct variation is a relationship between two variables where one variable is a constant multiple of the other.
pg013_n0006: In other words, if one variable increases or decreases, the other variable changes proportionally in the same direction.
pg013_n0008: This type of variation is useful for understanding how changes in one variable affect another in a directly proportional manner.
pg013_n0010: Engage in Activity 1.3 to explore the application of direct variation in real life.
pg013_n0012: If <math><mi>y</mi></math> is directly proportional to <math><mi>x</mi></math>, it can be written as <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∝</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, where <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∝</mo></math> is a symbol of proportionality.
pg013_n0013: The corresponding mathematical equation connecting <math><mi>x</mi></math> and <math><mi>y</mi></math> is formed by introducing a proportionality constant <math><mi>k</mi></math>, and replaces <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∝</mo></math> with an equal sign to get, <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
pg013_n0015: For instance, if <math><mi>y</mi></math> varies directly as the square of <math><mi>x</mi></math>, then <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∝</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup></mrow></math> and the corresponding equation is <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup></mrow></math>, where <math><mi>k</mi></math> is the constant of proportionality.
pg013_n0017: For any two pairs of quantities <math><mi>x</mi></math> and <math><mi>y</mi></math>, say <math><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, two equations <math><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> are obtained.
pg013_n0019: So, it is said that <math><mi>x</mi></math> and <math><mi>y</mi></math> vary directly if the ratios of the values of <math><mi>y</mi></math> to the values of <math><mi>x</mi></math> are proportional.
pg013_n0021: If <math><mi>x</mi></math> and <math><mi>y</mi></math> are any two quantities that are in direct variation, then <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
pg013_n0022: The nature of the equation <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is a straight line passing through the origin, where <math><mi>k</mi></math> represents the gradient (slope) of the line.

pg016_n0005: A relationship between two or more variables is said to be an inverse variation if the value of one variable increases while the other value decreases, or vice versa.
pg016_n0006: Engage in Activity 1.4 to explore further inverse variations.
pg016_n0008: Quantities with an inverse variation relationship are said to be inversely proportional to each other.
pg016_n0009: In this case, the quantities vary inversely or in inverse proportion.
pg016_n0010: Inverse proportion is sometimes referred to as indirect proportion.
pg016_n0012: For example, the number of men employed to cultivate a farm and time taken to complete the work are inversely related.
pg016_n0013: Likewise, the time to travel to a certain place and the speed are inversely related.

pg026_n0009: In fields like architecture, engineering and design, precise measurements and patterns are crucial.
pg026_n0010: Maintaining such patterns and measurements across objects and designs requires an understanding of the relationship between shapes and their properties.
pg026_n0011: In this chapter, you will learn about postulates, proofs and theorems on congruence as well as the congruence of triangles.
pg026_n0012: The competencies developed will enable you to solve problems such as determining the dimensions of sides of figures without taking actual measurements, designing and making objects of the same shapes and sizes such as worn-out parts.
pg026_n0017: Without knowledge of congruence industries would take longer time to produce objects of the same shape and size.
pg026_n0021: The term congruence is derived from the Latin word congruentia which means agree or fit together exactly.
pg026_n0022: Engage in Activity 2.1 to explore the characteristics of objects from real life situations which fit together.

pg026_n0037: In Activity 2.1, one may have noticed that same objects matched exactly on top of each other.
pg026_n0038: This means that the objects have the same shape and size.
pg026_n0039: Two or more objects with such characteristics are called congruent figures.
pg026_n0043: Understanding postulates, theorems, and proofs is important for developing a solid foundation in mathematics.
pg026_n0044: These concepts form the basis for logical reasoning and they are used to validate mathematical ideas.
pg027_n0007: A postulate is a statement that is accepted as true without any proof.
pg027_n0008: These statements are universally accepted, self-evident and can form the basis for further reasoning and making arguments.
pg027_n0009: The following are examples of postulates.
pg027_n0013: A circle can be drawn with any centre and radius.
pg027_n0016: A straight line can be drawn from any point to any other point.
pg027_n0019: All right angles are equal to each other.
pg027_n0023: A theorem is an argument that has been proved to be true based on past established results, definitions or postulates.
pg027_n0024: The following are examples of theorems.
pg027_n0028: The sum of interior angles of a triangle is 180 degrees.
pg027_n0031: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the length of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other two sides.
pg027_n0034: The sum of interior angles of a quadrilateral is 360 degrees.
pg027_n0038: A proof is a series of logical statements that are based on definitions, previously established facts, and postulates that may be used to conclude the truth of a mathematical argument.
pg027_n0039: The following are common procedures when undertaking a proof.
pg027_n0043: Draw a clearly labelled diagram to represent a problem.
pg027_n0044: Indicate all the information such as equal angles, parallel lines, and congruent segments.
pg027_n0047: Write down the given information based on the labels of the supporting figures.
pg027_n0050: State the argument which needs to be proved.
pg027_n0053: Where necessary, make additional constructions with dotted lines to make the proof clear.
pg027_n0060: Refer the figures you have planned to use in the proof.
pg027_n0063: Provide arguments with reasons based on the given information or established facts.
pg027_n0066: Start with statements whose validity are given or are obvious.
pg027_n0069: The final statement is the conclusion about what was supposed to be proved.

pg041_n0017: A postulate is a statement that is accepted without any proof.
pg041_n0021: A theorem is an argument that has been proven to be true based on past established results or definitions or postulates.

pg041_n0033: The sides of one triangle have equal lengths to the corresponding sides of the other triangle (SSS).

pg041_n0039: Two angles and the included side of one triangle are respectively equal to the corresponding two angles and the included side of the other triangle (ASA).
pg041_n0042: Two angles and non-included side of one triangle are respectively equal to the corresponding two angles and a non-included side of the other triangle (AAS).
pg041_n0046: Two right-angled triangles are congruent if their hypotenuses and a pair of sides have equal length (RHS).

pg067_n0007: Skills in solving problems systematically, logically, and making connections between variables are essential in daily life.
pg067_n0008: Such skills can be developed and applied by learning algebra.
pg067_n0009: In this chapter, you will learn about binary operations, quadratic expressions, and solving quadratic equations.
pg067_n0010: The competencies developed will enable you to solve daily life problems such as budgeting, comparing prices, planning for a journey and figuring proportions in cooking.
pg067_n0011: Also, algebra is useful in other subjects and fields such as science, engineering and technology and many other applications.
pg067_n0014: The role algebra plays in real life.
pg067_n0017: A binary operation is a rule for combining two quantities to produce a unique quantity from the same set.
pg067_n0018: It makes use of symbols that represent one or more operations.
pg067_n0020: The symbols used in binary operations are not standard, this means, they do not represent a specific operation.
pg067_n0021: A symbol may be used in a certain operation in an expression, and yet have a different meaning in another expression.
pg067_n0023: A binary operation may be denoted by symbols such as Δ and *, depending on the instructions given for the operation.
pg067_n0025: The instructions may be given in words or by symbols.
pg067_n0026: Binary operations may involve the basic arithmetic operations such as addition (+), subtraction (−), multiplication (×), and division (÷) depending on the given definition.
pg067_n0027: Engage in Activity 4.1 to learn more on binary operations.

pg070_n0019: A formula is an equation which shows how variables are related.
pg070_n0020: For example, the formula which is used to find the circumference, <math><mi>C</mi></math> of a circle is given by <math><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, where <math><mi>C</mi></math> is expressed in terms of <math><mi>π</mi></math> and <math><mi>d</mi></math>.
pg070_n0021: In this case, <math><mi>C</mi></math> is the subject of the formula.
pg070_n0022: It is also possible to express <math><mi>d</mi></math> as the subject of the formula, that is, <math><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mi>C</mi><mi>π</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></math>.
pg070_n0024: The procedure of expressing a formula in different ways is called transposition of formula or changing subject of the formula.

pg072_n0049: An expression whose highest exponent (degree) of the variable is 2 is called a quadratic expression.
pg072_n0051: The following are examples of quadratic expressions:
pg072_n0055: <math><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>z</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, the highest exponent (or degree) of <math><mi>z</mi></math> is 2.
pg072_n0063: In general, a quadratic expression has the form <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>, where <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and <math><mi>a</mi></math>, <math><mi>b</mi></math>, and <math><mi>c</mi></math> are real numbers.
pg072_n0064: The term <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup></mrow></math> is called the quadratic term, where <math><mi>a</mi></math> is the coefficient of <math><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup></math>.
pg072_n0065: The term <math><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is called the linear term (middle term), where <math><mi>b</mi></math> is the coefficient of <math><mi>x</mi></math> and <math><mi>c</mi></math> is the constant term.
pg072_n0067: For example, in the quadratic expression <math><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>, the coefficient of <math><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup></math> is 4, the coefficient of <math><mi>x</mi></math> is <math><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> and the constant is 7.
pg072_n0069: Engage Activity 4.2 and learn how to deduce quadratic expressions from real life situations.
pg072_n0072: Activity 4.2: Deducing quadratic expressions from real life
pg072_n0075: A garden designer plans to design different gardens in a compound.
pg072_n0076: During an investigation, he noticed that the length of each garden is 4 m longer than its width.
pg072_n0077: Deduce the simplest possible expression of the area of the garden by expanding the factors.
pg072_n0079: Explore various sources to learn more about how you can expand such results.
pg072_n0081: Make a presentation to demonstrate how you arrived at your conclusion.
pg072_n0083: From Activity 4.2, it can be observed that, quadratic expressions can be derived from the product of two linear expressions.

pg073_n0032: Thus, <math><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> is the expanded form of <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.

pg073_n0034: Therefore, <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>.
pg073_n0036: The expression <math><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> is called a quadratic expression expanded from <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.

pg074_n0004: Note that, from the general quadratic expression <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>, where <math><mi>a</mi></math>, <math><mi>b</mi></math> and <math><mi>c</mi></math> are real numbers.
pg074_n0007: For example, <math><mrow><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>, in this case, <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, <math><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>.

pg075_n0006: Factorisation is the process of writing an expression as a product of its factors.
pg075_n0007: Numbers and algebraic expressions can be expressed in terms of factors.
pg075_n0008: For instance, 10 can be expressed as a product of 2 and 5 or 1 and 10.
pg075_n0010: The expression <math><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math> can be expressed as a product of two linear factors <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>.
pg075_n0011: That is, <math><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
pg075_n0013: Quadratic expressions can be factored using three main methods which are splitting the middle term, difference of two squares and perfect squares.
pg075_n0015: Factorisation by splitting the middle term
pg075_n0017: Factorisation by splitting the middle term involves the splitting of the middle term into two terms.
pg075_n0018: For instance, in the quadratic expression <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>, the middle term is <math><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
pg075_n0019: To split the middle term, the following steps can be used:
pg075_n0022: (i) Find two numbers whose sum is equal to <math><mi>b</mi></math> and whose product is equal to <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>.
pg075_n0024: (ii) To find the two numbers in (i), list all the factors of <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> and determine a pair whose sum is <math><mi>b</mi></math>.

pg077_n0055: A quadratic expression whose factor are identical is called a perfect square.

This shows that in a perfect square trinomial the middle term is twice the product of the first term and the square root of the last term, and the constant term is the square of half the coefficient of the middle term.
pg078_sec002_ans_item-3: In general, (a + b)<math><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math> = <math><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> + 2ab + <math><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> and (a - b)<math><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math> = <math><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> - 2ab + <math><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>. Therefore a perfect square trinomial has first and last terms that are squares, while the middle term is plus or minus twice the product of their square roots. pg083_n0063: Solving quadratic equations by completing the square
pg083_n0065: In the previous section, a method for solving quadratic equations by splitting the middle term was discussed.
pg083_n0066: However, not all quadratic equations can be factored.

pg083_n0068: For such equations, methods such as completing the square and quadratic formula can be used.

pg092_n0019: From Activity 5.1, one may have explored various ways used to express numbers.
pg092_n0020: One of the common methods of expressing numbers is by multiplying the same or different numbers several times.
pg093_n0014: These are expanded form of numbers.
pg093_n0016: From the given examples, some numbers can be expressed in short form by counting the number of times the same number is multiplied and writing the result on the top right hand of the multiplied number.
pg093_n0020: (i) 4 = 2 × 2 = <math><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></math> since 2 is multiplied repeatedly two times.
pg093_n0022: (ii) 8 = 2 × 2 × 2 = <math><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></math> since 2 is multiplied repeatedly three times.
pg093_n0024: (iii) 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 = <math><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> since 2 is multiplied repeatedly two times, and three is multiplied once.
pg093_n0026: (iv) 81 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = <math><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></math> since 3 is multiplied repeatedly four times.
pg093_n0028: Numbers expressed in the forms <math><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></math>, <math><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></math> and <math><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></math> are called powers.
pg093_n0029: The numbers which are multiplied several times are called bases, and the number of times any number is multiplied by itself is called exponent.
pg093_n0036: Likewise, <math><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>5</mn></msup></math> is read as the “fifth power of 3” or “3 raised to exponent five” and <math><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></math> is read as the “third power of 2” or “2 raised to exponent 3”.
pg093_n0038: Engage in Activity 5.2 to explore more about exponential numbers.

pg096_n0040: There are three groups of exponents namely positive, negative, and zero exponents.
pg096_n0041: Simplification of the exponents are usually based on the four laws called multiplication, division, power, and zero power.

pg096_n0052: Count how many times 5 is multiplied by itself.
pg096_n0053: The answer is five times, which gives the exponent.
pg096_n0054: Thus, 5 is multiplied by itself five times.
pg096_n0055: The exponent 5 can also be obtained by adding the exponents from each base.

pg096_n0063: Generally, if x is any non-zero number with positive exponents m and n, then <math><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi class="tml-sml-pad">m</mi></msup><mo>×</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi class="tml-sml-pad">n</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow class="tml-sml-pad"><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

pg101_n0038: An expression <math><mfrac><msup><mn>7</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><msup><mn>7</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac></math> can be simplified by using the division law of exponents as follows:
pg101_n0039: <math><mrow><mfrac><msup><mn>7</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><msup><mn>7</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="2em"></mspace><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
pg101_n0040: <math><mrow><mtext>Alternatively, </mtext><mfrac><msup><mn>7</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><msup><mn>7</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>7</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>7</mn><mn>0</mn></msup><mi>.</mi><mspace width="2em"></mspace><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
pg101_n0042: From equations (1) and (2), it follows that <math><mrow><msup><mn>7</mn><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
pg101_n0043: Similarly, if <math><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, then <math><mrow><mfrac><msup><mi>m</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><msup><mi>m</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> <math><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
pg101_n0044: Thus, <math><mrow><mfrac><msup><mi>m</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><msup><mi>m</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></mrow></math> <math><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
pg101_n0047: Generally, if <math><mi>x</mi></math> is any non-zero number, then <math><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">0</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. In this case <math><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>0</mn></msup></math> is not defined.

pg101_n0054: <math><mrow><mtext>Also, </mtext><mfrac><msup><mn>8</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><msup><mn>8</mn><mn>5</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>8</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>8</mn><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>.</mi><mspace width="2em"></mspace><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
pg101_n0056: Comparing equations (1) and (2), gives <math><mrow><msup><mn>8</mn><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>8</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow></math>.

pg102_n0014: When <math><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, <math><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow class="tml-sml-pad"><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow class="tml-sml-pad"><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">1</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>x</mi></mfrac></mrow></math>.

pg103_im006: Worked example (b) simplifies the expression a^<math><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> divided by <math><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mn>0</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> using the law of indices for division. The steps subtract exponents to give a^-<math><mrow><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow></math>, then rewrite this as (<math><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>6</mn></msup></math>)/(<math><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>6</mn></msup></math>), and finally as (b/a)<math><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>6</mn></msup></math>. The concluding statement is a^<math><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> over <math><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mn>0</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> equals (b/a)<math><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>6</mn></msup></math>.
pg103_im007: Worked example (c) simplifies the product (-2a^2b^-2c)<math><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></math>(3ab^<math><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>c</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">5</mn></msup></mrow></math>)(xyz)<math><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>0</mn></msup></math>. Since (xyz)<math><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>0</mn></msup></math> equals 1, the working expands the powers, combines like bases, and rewrites positive exponents in negative-index form. pg116_n0020: Rationalisation of a denominator involves eliminating radicals from the denominator of a fraction.
pg116_n0021: This makes denominator, to be a rational number.
pg116_n0022: The procedure for rationalising the denominator are as follows:
pg116_n0024: (i) If the denominator is a single radical term, multiply the numerator and the denominator by the radical in the denominator.
pg116_n0025: For example, in rationalising the denominator of <math><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mi>a</mi><msqrt><mi>b</mi></msqrt></mfrac></mstyle></math>, multiplying both the numerator and denominator by <math><msqrt><mi>b</mi></msqrt></math> as follow.
pg116_n0029: (ii) If the denominator is a sum or difference of two radicals, change the sign connecting the two terms.
pg116_n0030: The resulting expression is called the rationalising factor, which is then multiplied in the numerator and the denominator.
pg116_n0031: For example, in rationalizing the denominator of <math><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>a</mi><mspace width="0pt" height="0.5em"></mspace></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mi>b</mi></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></math>, the rationalising factor is <math><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>a</mi><mspace width="0pt" height="0.5em"></mspace></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mi>b</mi></msqrt></mrow></math>.
pg116_n0032: Multiply both the numerator and the denominator by <math><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>a</mi><mspace width="0pt" height="0.5em"></mspace></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mi>b</mi></msqrt></mrow></math> as follows.
pg116_n0033: <math><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>a</mi><mspace width="0pt" height="0.5em"></mspace></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mi>b</mi></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>a</mi><mspace width="0pt" height="0.5em"></mspace></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mi>b</mi></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>×</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>a</mi><mspace width="0pt" height="0.5em"></mspace></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mi>b</mi></msqrt></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>a</mi><mspace width="0pt" height="0.5em"></mspace></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mi>b</mi></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>a</mi><mspace width="0pt" height="0.5em"></mspace></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mi>b</mi></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></math>

pg124_n0012: Some real life situations such as earthquakes, population growth, and levels of acid or alkali in liquids are associated with very large or very small numbers.
pg124_n0013: In such cases, describing such situations becomes difficult.
pg124_n0014: However the concept of logarithm has made such descriptions easy for an individual to understand the effects of their occurrences.
pg124_n0015: In this chapter, you will learn to write numbers in standard form and use laws of logarithms to solve problems.
pg124_n0016: The competencies developed will enable you to simplify and find solutions to complex expressions, solve problems related to exponential growth decay, and understand the science of earthquakes and the spread of diseases, and many other applications.

pg124_n0040: When writing numbers in standard form, the following must be considered:
pg124_n0044: For numbers between 0 and 1, move the decimal point towards right until a number between 1 and 10 is obtained and the exponent of 10 is negative.
pg124_n0047: For numbers greater than or equal to 10, move the decimal point left until the value is between 1 and 10, resulting in a positive exponent of 10.
pg124_n0050: The exponent of 10 is determined by the number of places the decimal point is moved, either to the right or left.
pg125_n0007: For the numbers which are between 1 and less than 10, the exponent of 10 is 0.
pg125_n0011: In multiplication of numbers in standard form, the exponents are added, while in division the exponents are subtracted.

pg128_n0006: When a number is expressed in power form, it is written as a base raised to an exponent.
pg128_n0007: For instance, if <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></mrow></math>, then ‘a’ is written in terms of base ‘b’ raised to an exponent ‘x’ or ‘x’ is the logarithm of <math><mi>a</mi></math> to base <math><mi>b</mi></math>.
pg128_n0009: The exponent <math><mi>x</mi></math> is the number that shows how many times a base is multiplied by itself to obtain a product.
pg128_n0010: Thus, <math><mi>x</mi></math> is called the logarithm of <math><mi>a</mi></math> to base <math><mi>b</mi></math>.
pg128_n0011: Symbolically, this is written as <math><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, where <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, <math><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
pg128_n0012: This notation is called logarithmic notation.
pg128_n0013: For instance, 64 in exponential form can be expressed as <math><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow></math>.
pg128_n0014: The exponent 6 is called the logarithm of 64 to base 2, written as <math><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mn>64</mn></mrow></math>.

pg128_n0027: In general, <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></mrow></math> is written as <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> where <math><mi>a</mi></math> and <math><mi>b</mi></math> are positive real numbers and <math><mi>x</mi></math> is a real number, <math><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.

pg139_n0029: An antilogarithm of a number is the inverse process of finding a number whose logarithm is known.

pg146_n0008: Objects exist in different categories and characteristics which sometimes may be difficult to describe and understand their nature.
pg146_n0009: Understanding the concepts of sets simplifies the process of categorising and organising such objects based on their nature.
pg146_n0010: In this chapter, you will learn the concept of a set, distinguish between types of sets, perform operations with sets, represent sets in Venn diagrams, and determine the number of elements in a set.
pg146_n0011: The competencies developed will enable you to simplify, categorise, analyse, and generalise different problems arising from real-life situations more systematically.
pg146_n0014: Organising and categorising data with little or no knowledge about the concepts of sets.
pg146_n0018: A set is a collection of well defined objects with common and distinct features.
pg146_n0019: The objects in a set are called elements or members of the set.
pg146_n0020: The members of a set are usually separated by commas and enclosed within curly brackets { }.
pg146_n0021: For instance, if B is a set representing students in a class and John is a student in that class, then John is a member of set B or is an element of set B.
pg146_n0022: This relationship is denoted by the symbol ∈, which means ‘a member of’ or ‘an element of’.
pg146_n0024: For example, if C = {1, 2, 3}, then 1∈C, 2∈C, and 3∈C whereas 5∉C (5 is not an element of C).
pg146_n0025: The number of distinct elements in set A is represented by <math><mrow><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
pg146_n0026: For example, if A = {a, e, i, o, u}, then <math><mrow><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>.

pg147_n0003: Sets can be described in different ways.
pg147_n0004: The most common ways of describing a set are: by statement form, by listing (roster form), and by a formula (set builder notation).
pg147_n0005: For instance, if set A is a set of even numbers, then it can be described as follows:

pg147_n0010: and is read as A is the set of all x such that x is an even number.

pg148_n0054: Sets can be categorised into different types based on the number and nature of their elements.
pg148_n0055: The categories include: finite, infinite, singleton, and empty sets.
pg148_n0059: A set is finite if it contains a countable number of elements.
pg148_n0060: For instance, A = {a, b, c, d, e} is a finite set because its elements can be counted.
pg148_n0064: A set is infinite if it contains an uncountable number of elements.
pg148_n0065: When representing infinite sets, a few elements are listed followed by an ellipsis (…) to indicate that the list does not have an end.
pg148_n0066: For instance, A = {2, 4, 6, 8, } is an infinite set because the entire elements cannot be counted.
pg148_n0070: An empty set is a set which has no elements.
pg148_n0071: It is also called as a null or void set.
pg148_n0072: For instance, the set of prime numbers between 31 and 37 is an empty set because there is no prime number between 31 and 37.
pg148_n0073: An empty set is denoted by the symbol { } or Ø.
pg148_n0077: A singleton set is a set that contains only one element.
pg148_n0082: Two or more sets can be compared and classified as equivalent sets, equal sets or one is a subset of the other.
pg148_n0086: Two sets are equivalent if they have the same number of elements.
pg148_n0087: Normally, the symbol "≡" is used to denote equivalent.
pg148_n0088: For instance, set A = {2, 4, 6, 8} and set B = {a, b, c, d} are equivalent because they have equal number of elements.
pg148_n0089: That is, <math><mrow><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>.
pg149_n0004: Generally, if <math><mrow><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, then the sets A and B are said to be equivalent.
pg149_n0010: Show that <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>4</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mpadded lspace="0"><mi>goat</mi></mpadded><mo separator="true">,</mo><mpadded lspace="0"><mi>dog</mi></mpadded><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> are equivalent.
pg149_n0013: Since <math><mrow><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, then, <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>≡</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
pg149_n0014: Therefore, the sets A and B are equivalent.
pg149_n0018: Two sets, A and B are said to be equal if they are equivalent and their members are exactly the same regardless of the arrangement or order.
pg149_n0019: For example, if <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>3</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, then <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> since all elements of A are elements of B and all elements of B are also elements of A.
pg149_n0022: All equal sets are equivalent but not all equivalent sets are equal.
pg149_n0027: If <math><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0.2222em" rspace="0.2222em">:</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0.2222em" rspace="0.2222em">:</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℤ</mi><mtext> and </mtext><mn>7</mn><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>10</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, show that <math><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>≡</mo><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>.

pg149_n0034: Hence, <math><mrow><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
pg149_n0037: Again, <math><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0.2222em" rspace="0.2222em">:</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℤ</mi><mtext> and </mtext><mn>7</mn><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>10</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
pg149_n0038: = <math><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>8</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>, <math><mtext> thus </mtext></math> n(Q) = 2.

pg150_n0032: Set A is a subset of another set B if all elements of A are also elements of B.
pg150_n0033: For example, if A = {a, b, c, e} and B = {a, b, c, d, e}, then A is a subset of B because all elements of A belong to B.
pg150_n0034: If A has less elements than B, then A is called a proper subset of B, denoted by A ⊂ B.
pg150_n0035: If A is a subset of B and the two sets are equal, then A is called an improper subset of B, written as A ⊆ B.
pg150_n0036: If A = B, then A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.
pg150_n0038: Therefore, a subset of a set can either be proper or improper.

pg153_n0025: Set operations are categorized into four types namely: union, intersection, complement, and set difference.
pg153_n0026: These operations involve identifying elements in each set and determining the number of elements involved.
pg153_n0030: The union of two or more sets is the set that contains all the elements of each set, without any repetition.
pg153_n0031: The union of sets is represented by the cup symbol "∪".
pg153_n0032: Thus, A∪B denotes that an element x belongs to A∪B if and only if x∈A or x∈B or x is in both A and B.

pg153_n0052: The intersection of sets, A and B is the set which contains all the elements that are common to both sets.
pg153_n0053: It is denoted by the cap symbol “∩”.

pg158_n0016: A set can be represented by a diagram called a Venn diagram.
pg158_n0017: A Venn diagram is named after a British Mathematician, John Venn.
pg158_n0018: In drawing Venn diagrams, rectangles represent universal sets, while ovals or circles represent subsets.
pg158_n0019: For instance, the set <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mtext> </mtext><mi>b</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mtext> </mtext><mi>c</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> can be represented in a Venn diagram as shown in Figure 7.1.

pg158_n0021: Figure 7.1: Venn diagram for set A
pg158_n0023: In this case, <math><mi>μ</mi></math> represents the universal set and <math><mi>A</mi></math> is a subset of <math><mi>μ</mi></math>.
pg158_n0024: If two sets have elements in common, their ovals overlap.
pg158_n0025: For instance, if <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, then the representation of the sets A and B in a Venn diagram is as shown in Figure 7.2.
pg158_im006: Venn diagram of universal set μ with two intersecting sets, A on the left and B on the right. The intersection A ∩ B contains elements a and b, element c lies in A only, and element d lies in B only.
pg158_n0027: Figure 7.2: Joint sets in a Venn diagram
pg158_n0029: If the sets are disjoint, the circles or ovals do not overlap.
pg158_n0030: For instance, if <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, the Venn diagram for the two disjoint sets is shown in Figure 7.3.

pg168_n0009: Accurate measurements such as distances, angles, and navigation would be difficult without having the knowledge of trigonometry.
pg168_n0010: In this chapter, you will learn trigonometric ratios, trigonometric ratios of special angles, trigonometric ratios of any angle, inverses of trigonometric ratios and perform calculations that involve angles of elevation and depression.

pg168_n0018: Sine, cosine, and tangent are the basic trigonometric ratios abbreviated as ‘sin’, ‘cos’, and ‘tan’.
pg168_n0019: These are referred to as ratios because they are defined by ratios of the sides of a right-angled triangle.
pg168_n0020: Other trigonometric ratios derived from these basic ratios are secant, cosecant, and cotangent.
pg168_n0021: These are reciprocals of the three basic trigonometric ratios.

pg192_n0028: The angles of elevation and depression
pg192_n0030: When observing an object, you can either observe it horizontally if the object and line of sight are at the same level.
pg192_n0031: Observing it downward if the observer is above the object and observing it upwards if the observer is below the observed object.
pg192_n0032: To experience these scenarios, engage in Activity 8.5.
pg192_n0035: Activity 8.5: Studying different angles formed when observing objects
pg192_n0039: At your place, choose an object to observe which is at the same level as your eyes.
pg192_n0040: For instance, a person whose height is the same as yours and you look at his eyes.
pg192_n0043: In the second scenario, observe an object which you need to look downward.
pg192_n0044: For instance, looking at a coin on the floor while standing.
pg193_n0006: In the third scenario, observe an object which is at a position which you need to look upwards.
pg193_n0007: For instance, looking at the top of the building.
pg193_n0010: Study and reflect on all three cases and discover features such as angles formed, and possibilities of determining distances between the observer and the objects without measurements.
pg193_n0013: Use the internet or other relevant sources to study and justify your observations and share your findings through visual diagrams.
pg193_n0015: In Activity 8.5, it can be deduced that observing an object below or above the horizontal level, the line of sight forms an angle below or above.
pg193_n0016: An angle formed between a horizontal level and a line of sight by observing an object downward is called an angle of depression.
pg193_n0017: The angle formed by observing an object upwards is called an angle of elevation.

pg012_n0037_easy_read:
Variation is a relationship between 2 quantities.
When 1 quantity changes, the other quantity changes in proportion.
pg012_n0038_easy_read: Variation helps us explore connections between 2 or more quantities.
pg012_n0039_easy_read:
The 4 basic types of variation are:
- direct
- inverse
- joint
- combined
pg013_n0005_easy_read:
Direct variation is a relationship between 2 variables.
In this relationship, 1 variable is a constant multiple of the other variable.
pg013_n0006_easy_read: In other words, if 1 variable increases or decreases, the other variable also changes in the same direction and in proportion.
pg013_n0008_easy_read: This type of variation helps us understand how a change in 1 variable affects another variable in direct proportion.
pg013_n0010_easy_read:
Do Activity 1.3.
Explore how direct variation is used in real life.
pg013_n0012_easy_read:
If <math><mi>y</mi></math> is directly proportional to <math><mi>x</mi></math>, we write it as <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∝</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
The symbol <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∝</mo></math> means "is proportional to."
pg013_n0013_easy_read:
The equation that connects <math><mi>x</mi></math> and <math><mi>y</mi></math> uses a proportionality constant <math><mi>k</mi></math>.
Replace <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∝</mo></math> with an equal sign.
Then the equation is <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
pg013_n0015_easy_read:
For example, if <math><mi>y</mi></math> varies directly as the square of <math><mi>x</mi></math>, then <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∝</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup></mrow></math>.
The matching equation is <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup></mrow></math>.
Here, <math><mi>k</mi></math> is the constant of proportionality.
pg013_n0017_easy_read:
Take any 2 pairs of quantities <math><mi>x</mi></math> and <math><mi>y</mi></math>, such as <math><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Then we get 2 equations:
- <math><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math>
- <math><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math>
pg013_n0019_easy_read: So, <math><mi>x</mi></math> and <math><mi>y</mi></math> vary directly when the ratios of the values of <math><mi>y</mi></math> to the values of <math><mi>x</mi></math> are proportional.
pg013_n0021_easy_read: If <math><mi>x</mi></math> and <math><mi>y</mi></math> are in direct variation, then <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
pg013_n0022_easy_read:
The equation <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> makes a straight line that passes through the origin.
In this equation, <math><mi>k</mi></math> is the gradient, or slope, of the line.
pg013_n0027_easy_read:
Figure 1.1 shows this:
If quantity <math><mi>x</mi></math> increases, quantity <math><mi>y</mi></math> also increases in proportion.
If quantity <math><mi>x</mi></math> decreases, quantity <math><mi>y</mi></math> also decreases in proportion.
The same idea also works the other way round.

pg016_n0009_easy_read: In this case, the quantities vary inversely, or in inverse proportion.
pg016_n0010_easy_read: Inverse proportion is also sometimes called indirect proportion.
pg016_n0012_easy_read: For example, the number of men working on a farm and the time needed to finish the work are inversely related.
pg016_n0013_easy_read: In the same way, travel time to a place and speed are inversely related.

pg067_n0017_easy_read: A binary operation is a rule that combines 2 quantities to make 1 unique quantity from the same set.
pg067_n0018_easy_read: A binary operation uses symbols to show 1 or more operations.
pg067_n0020_easy_read: The symbols used in binary operations are not standard. This means they do not show 1 specific operation.
pg067_n0021_easy_read: A symbol may mean 1 operation in one expression, but it may mean a different operation in another expression.
pg067_n0023_easy_read: A binary operation may use symbols such as Δ and *. This depends on the instructions given for the operation.
pg067_n0025_easy_read: The instructions may be given in words or with symbols.
pg067_n0026_easy_read:
Binary operations may include basic arithmetic operations, depending on the definition, such as:
- addition (+)
- subtraction (−)
- multiplication (×)
- division (÷)

pg070_n0020_easy_read:
For example, you can find the circumference <math><mi>C</mi></math> of a circle with the formula <math><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>.
In this formula, <math><mi>C</mi></math> is written using <math><mi>π</mi></math> and <math><mi>d</mi></math>.
pg070_n0021_easy_read: Here, <math><mi>C</mi></math> is the subject of the formula.
pg070_n0022_easy_read:
You can also make <math><mi>d</mi></math> the subject of the formula.
Then the formula is <math><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mi>C</mi><mi>π</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></math>.
pg070_n0024_easy_read:
Writing a formula in different ways is called transposition of formula.
It is also called changing the subject of the formula.
pg070_n0025_easy_read: Here are some examples of formulae:
pg070_n0038_easy_read: Given that <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>, make <math><mi>m</mi></math> the subject of the formula.
pg070_n0044_easy_read:
Subtract <math><mi>c</mi></math> from both sides of equation (i).
You get:
<math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> (ii)
pg070_n0046_easy_read:
Divide all of equation (ii) by <math><mi>x</mi></math>.
You get:
<math><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mi>x</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></math>
pg070_n0053_easy_read:
The volume of a cylinder is <math><mi>V</mi></math>.
The base has radius <math><mi>r</mi></math>.
The height is <math><mi>h</mi></math>.
The formula is <math><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup><mi>h</mi></mrow></math>.
pg070_n0054_easy_read: Make <math><mi>r</mi></math> the subject of the formula.
pg071_n0005_easy_read:
Divide both sides of equation (i) by <math><mrow><mi>π</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math>.
You get <math><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup></mrow></math>.
pg071_n0008_easy_read:
Apply the square root to both sides of equation (ii).
You get <math><mrow><msqrt><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>.
pg071_n0015_easy_read: Given that <math><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><msqrt><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mi>l</mi><mi>g</mi></mfrac></mstyle></msqrt></mrow></math>, make <math><mi>l</mi></math> the subject of the formula.
pg071_n0022_easy_read:
Divide both sides of equation (i) by <math><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow></math>.
You get <math><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mi>T</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mi>l</mi><mi>g</mi></mfrac></mstyle></msqrt></mrow></math>.
pg071_n0025_easy_read:
Square both sides of equation (ii).
You get <math><mrow><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="true">(</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mi>T</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mi>l</mi><mi>g</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></math>.
pg071_n0028_easy_read:
Multiply both sides of equation (iii) by <math><mi>g</mi></math>.
You get <math><mrow><mi>g</mi><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="true">(</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mi>T</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></math>.
pg071_n0030_easy_read: Also, <math><mrow><mi>g</mi><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="true">(</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mi>T</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mrow><mi>g</mi><msup><mi>T</mi><mn class="tml-med-pad">2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></math>.
pg071_n0037_easy_read:
The formula for simple interest is <math><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow><mn>100</mn></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></math>.
Here, <math><mi>I</mi></math> is the simple interest, <math><mi>P</mi></math> is the principal, <math><mi>T</mi></math> is the time in years, and <math><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> is the rate per annum.
pg071_n0038_easy_read: Make <math><mi>P</mi></math> the subject of the formula.
pg071_n0045_easy_read:
Multiply both sides of equation (i) by 100.
You get <math><mrow><mn>100</mn><mi>I</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>.
pg071_n0048_easy_read:
Divide both sides of equation (ii) by <math><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>.
You get <math><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mrow><mn>100</mn><mi>I</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>.

pg072_n0049_easy_read: A quadratic expression is an expression where the highest exponent, or degree, of the variable is 2.
pg072_n0051_easy_read: These are examples of quadratic expressions:
pg072_n0055_easy_read:
<math><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>z</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
The highest exponent, or degree, of <math><mi>z</mi></math> is 2.
pg072_n0063_easy_read:
In general, a quadratic expression has the form <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>.
Here, <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
<math><mi>a</mi></math>, <math><mi>b</mi></math>, and <math><mi>c</mi></math> are real numbers.
pg072_n0064_easy_read:
The term <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup></mrow></math> is the quadratic term.
<math><mi>a</mi></math> is the coefficient of <math><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup></math>.
pg072_n0065_easy_read:
The term <math><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is the linear term, or middle term.
<math><mi>b</mi></math> is the coefficient of <math><mi>x</mi></math>.
<math><mi>c</mi></math> is the constant term.
pg072_n0067_easy_read:
For example, in the quadratic expression <math><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>:
- the coefficient of <math><msup><mi>x</mi><mn class="tml-sml-pad">2</mn></msup></math> is 4
- the coefficient of <math><mi>x</mi></math> is <math><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>
- the constant is 7

pg092_n0020_easy_read: One common way to write numbers is to multiply the same number or different numbers several times.
pg093_n0014_easy_read: These are expanded forms of numbers.
pg093_n0016_easy_read:

Count how many times the same number is multiplied.
Then write that number at the top right of the multiplied number.
pg093_n0020_easy_read: (i) 4 = 2 × 2 = <math><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></math> because 2 is multiplied by itself 2 times.
pg093_n0022_easy_read: (ii) 8 = 2 × 2 × 2 = <math><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></math> because 2 is multiplied by itself 3 times.
pg093_n0024_easy_read: (iii) 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 = <math><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> because 2 is multiplied by itself 2 times, and 3 is multiplied 1 time.
pg093_n0026_easy_read: (iv) 81 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = <math><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></math> because 3 is multiplied by itself 4 times.
pg093_n0028_easy_read: Numbers written as <math><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></math>, <math><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></math>, and <math><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></math> are called powers.
pg093_n0029_easy_read:
The number multiplied several times is called the base.
The number that shows how many times it is multiplied by itself is called the exponent.
pg093_n0036_easy_read:
Also, <math><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>5</mn></msup></math> is read as "the fifth power of 3" or "3 raised to exponent five".
And <math><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></math> is read as "the third power of 2" or "2 raised to exponent 3".

pg116_n0020_easy_read: Rationalisation of a denominator means removing radicals from the denominator of a fraction.
pg116_n0021_easy_read: This makes the denominator a rational number.
pg116_n0022_easy_read: The steps for rationalising the denominator are:
pg116_n0024_easy_read: (i) If the denominator has 1 radical term, multiply the numerator and the denominator by the radical in the denominator.
pg116_n0025_easy_read: For example, to rationalise the denominator of <math><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mi>a</mi><msqrt><mi>b</mi></msqrt></mfrac></mstyle></math>, multiply both the numerator and the denominator by <math><msqrt><mi>b</mi></msqrt></math> as follows.
pg116_n0029_easy_read: (ii) If the denominator has 2 radical terms added or subtracted, change the sign between the 2 terms.
pg116_n0030_easy_read:
This new expression is called the rationalising factor.
Then multiply the numerator and the denominator by it.

pg124_n0012_easy_read:
Some real-life situations use very large or very small numbers.
Examples are:
- earthquakes
- population growth
- levels of acid or alkali in liquids
pg124_n0013_easy_read: In these cases, it becomes difficult to describe the situations.
pg124_n0014_easy_read:
However, logarithms make these descriptions easier to understand.
They help a person understand their effects.
pg124_n0015_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn:
- to write numbers in standard form
- to use the laws of logarithms to solve problems
pg124_n0016_easy_read:
The skills you develop will help you:
- simplify complex expressions and find their solutions
- solve problems about exponential growth and decay
- understand the science of earthquakes
- understand the spread of diseases
- understand many other applications
pg124_n0020_easy_read:
It is hard to describe some real-life situations without knowing logarithms.
Examples are:
- the size of earthquakes
- the amount of acid and base in liquids
- population growth
pg124_n0024_easy_read:
A number is in standard form when it is written as <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math>.
In this form, <math><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>A</mi><mo><</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math> and <math><mi>n</mi></math> is an integer.
Standard form is also called scientific notation or standard notation.

pg124_n0040_easy_read: When you write numbers in standard form, remember these points:
pg124_n0044_easy_read:
For numbers between 0 and 1, move the decimal point to the right.
Stop when the number is between 1 and 10.
Then the exponent of 10 is negative.
pg124_n0047_easy_read:
For numbers that are 10 or more, move the decimal point to the left.
Stop when the number is between 1 and 10.
Then the exponent of 10 is positive.
pg124_n0050_easy_read:
The exponent of 10 depends on how many places you move the decimal point.
You may move it to the right or to the left.
pg125_n0007_easy_read: For numbers from 1 to less than 10, the exponent of 10 is 0.
pg125_n0011_easy_read:
When you multiply numbers in standard form, add the exponents.
When you divide numbers in standard form, subtract the exponents.

pg128_n0006_easy_read: A number in power form is written as a base with an exponent.
pg128_n0007_easy_read:
For example, if <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></mrow></math>,
then <math><mi>a</mi></math> is written with base <math><mi>b</mi></math> and exponent <math><mi>x</mi></math>.
Also, <math><mi>x</mi></math> is the logarithm of <math><mi>a</mi></math> to base <math><mi>b</mi></math>.
pg128_n0009_easy_read: The exponent <math><mi>x</mi></math> shows how many times the base is multiplied by itself to get the product.
pg128_n0010_easy_read: So, <math><mi>x</mi></math> is called the logarithm of <math><mi>a</mi></math> to base <math><mi>b</mi></math>.
pg128_n0011_easy_read:
This is written as <math><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
Here, <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, <math><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, and <math><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
pg128_n0012_easy_read: This way of writing is called logarithmic notation.
pg128_n0013_easy_read: For example, 64 in exponential form is <math><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow></math>.
pg128_n0014_easy_read:
The exponent 6 is the logarithm of 64 to base 2.
It is written as <math><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mn>64</mn></mrow></math>.

An antilogarithm is the opposite process.
You find the number when its logarithm is known.

pg146_n0008_easy_read: Objects belong to different categories and have different characteristics. Sometimes it is hard to describe them and understand their nature.
pg146_n0009_easy_read: Understanding sets makes it easier to categorise and organise these objects by their nature.
pg146_n0010_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn:
- the concept of a set
- different types of sets
- operations with sets
- how to show sets in Venn diagrams
- how to find the number of elements in a set
pg146_n0011_easy_read:
The skills you develop will help you:
- simplify problems
- categorise problems
- analyse problems
- generalise problems
These problems come from real-life situations. You will do this in a more systematic way.
pg146_n0014_easy_read: This means organising and categorising data with little or no knowledge of sets.
pg146_n0018_easy_read: A set is a collection of clearly defined objects with common and distinct features.
pg146_n0019_easy_read: The objects in a set are called elements or members of the set.
pg146_n0020_easy_read: The members of a set are usually separated by commas and put inside curly brackets { }.
pg146_n0021_easy_read: For example, B can be the set of students in a class. If John is a student in that class, then John is a member of set B. John is also an element of set B.
pg146_n0022_easy_read: This relationship is shown by the symbol ∈. It means "a member of" or "an element of".
pg146_n0024_easy_read:
For example, if C = {1, 2, 3}, then:
- 1∈C
- 2∈C
- 3∈C
But 5∉C. This means 5 is not an element of C.
pg146_n0025_easy_read: The number of distinct elements in set A is written as <math><mrow><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
pg146_n0026_easy_read: For example, if A = {a, e, i, o, u}, then <math><mrow><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>.

pg148_n0054_easy_read: Sets can be put into different types based on the number and kind of elements they have.
pg148_n0055_easy_read:
The types are:
- finite sets
- infinite sets
- singleton sets
- empty sets
pg148_n0059_easy_read: A set is finite if its elements can be counted.
pg148_n0060_easy_read: For example, A = {a, b, c, d, e} is a finite set because its elements can be counted.
pg148_n0064_easy_read: A set is infinite if its elements cannot be counted.
pg148_n0065_easy_read:
To show an infinite set, people write a few elements and then an ellipsis (…).
This shows that the list does not end.
pg148_n0066_easy_read: For example, A = {2, 4, 6, 8, } is an infinite set because all its elements cannot be counted.
pg148_n0070_easy_read: An empty set is a set with no elements.
pg148_n0071_easy_read: An empty set is also called a null set or a void set.
pg148_n0072_easy_read: For example, the set of prime numbers between 31 and 37 is an empty set because there is no prime number between 31 and 37.
pg148_n0073_easy_read: The symbol for an empty set is { } or Ø.
pg148_n0077_easy_read: A singleton set is a set with only 1 element.
pg148_n0082_easy_read:
You can compare 2 or more sets.
Then you can classify them as:
- equivalent sets
- equal sets
- one set is a subset of the other
pg148_n0086_easy_read: 2 sets are equivalent if they have the same number of elements.
pg148_n0088_easy_read: For example, set A = {2, 4, 6, 8} and set B = {a, b, c, d} are equivalent because they have the same number of elements.
pg148_n0089_easy_read: That is, <math><mrow><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>.
pg149_n0004_easy_read: In general, if <math><mrow><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, the sets A and B are equivalent.
pg149_n0010_easy_read: Show that <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>4</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mpadded lspace="0"><mi>goat</mi></mpadded><mo separator="true">,</mo><mpadded lspace="0"><mi>dog</mi></mpadded><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> are equivalent.
pg149_n0013_easy_read: Since <math><mrow><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>≡</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
pg149_n0014_easy_read: So, the sets A and B are equivalent.
pg149_n0018_easy_read: 2 sets, A and B, are equal if they are equivalent and have exactly the same members, in any order.
pg149_n0019_easy_read: For example, if <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>3</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, then <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>. pg230_n0009_easy_read: The measure of how far apart 2 straight lines are where they cross.
pg230_n0012_easy_read: The whole number part of a logarithm.
pg230_n0013_easy_read: It is the power of 10 when a number is written in scientific form.
pg230_n0016_easy_read: A polygon with equal angles at all vertices.
pg230_n0017_easy_read:
For example:
- a square
- an equilateral triangle
- a rectangle
pg230_n0020_easy_read: The longest side of a right-angled triangle.
pg230_n0021_easy_read: It is also the side opposite the right angle.
pg230_n0024_easy_read: Equations that are true for all values of the variable.
pg230_n0025_easy_read: This means that if you put any value of the unknown on both sides, both sides give the same number.
pg230_n0028_easy_read: A triangle with 2 sides of equal length.
pg230_n0031_easy_read: The part of a logarithm after the decimal point.
pg230_n0035_easy_read: An expression that says 1 quantity is a constant multiple of another quantity.
pg230_n0038_easy_read: A 4-sided polygon with 4 sides and 4 vertices.
pg230_n0041_easy_read: The inverse of a number. You usually get it by switching the numerator and the denominator.
pg230_n0044_easy_read: The ratio between matching measurements of the original object and the new object after enlargement.
pg230_n0045_easy_read: If the scale factor is greater than 1, the new figure is larger.
pg230_n0046_easy_read: If the scale factor is a fraction, the new figure is smaller.
pg230_n0047_easy_read: A scale factor is also called an enlargement factor.
pg230_n0050_easy_read: A plane with 2 coordinate axes, x and y, that are perpendicular.
pg230_n0051_easy_read: The x-axis is horizontal and the y-axis is vertical. They meet at a point called the origin.
